extraction.name: Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD)
extraction.description: SQuAD is a reading comprehension dataset consisting of 107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 Wikipedia articles, where the answer to each question is a segment of text (span) from the corresponding reading passage. It was created by crowdworkers and is designed to challenge machines on reading comprehension tasks.
extraction.creator: Pranav Rajpurkar, Jian Zhang, Konstantin Lopyrev, Percy Liang (Stanford University)
extraction.citeAs: Rajpurkar, P., Zhang, J., Lopyrev, K., & Liang, P. (2016). SQuAD: 100,000+ Questions for Machine Comprehension of Text. arXiv:1606.05250.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected in three stages: (1) passage curation from top 10,000 English Wikipedia articles using PageRank, sampling 536 articles; (2) crowdsourcing question-answer pairs via the Daemo platform with Amazon Mechanical Turk as backend, where workers asked and answered up to 5 questions per paragraph; (3) collecting at least 2 additional answers per question for development and test sets.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, User-generated content data, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: 2.6% of questions in the development and test sets were marked unanswerable by at least one of the additional crowdworkers.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Top 10,000 English Wikipedia articles ranked by Project Nayuki's Wikipedia internal PageRanks, from which 536 articles were sampled uniformly at random, yielding 23,215 paragraphs.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Paragraphs were extracted from Wikipedia articles by stripping away images, figures, tables, and discarding paragraphs shorter than 500 characters. Articles were partitioned randomly into training (80%), development (10%), and test (10%) sets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdworkers were tasked with asking and answering up to 5 questions per paragraph, entering questions in a text field and highlighting answers in the paragraph. Workers were encouraged to use their own words without copying phrases from the paragraph. Copy-paste functionality was disabled. For additional answers, workers selected the shortest span answering each question, or submitted without marking if unanswerable. Workers required 97% HIT acceptance rate, minimum 1000 HITs, and US/Canada location.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Daemo platform with Amazon Mechanical Turk as backend
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human performance was assessed by treating the second answer to each question as the human prediction and keeping other answers as ground truth. Human F1 was 86.8% on the test set. Mismatch occurred mostly due to inclusion/exclusion of non-essential phrases rather than fundamental disagreements.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 3 answers per question in development and test sets (1 original + at least 2 additional)
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowdworkers located in the United States or Canada, with a 97% HIT acceptance rate and a minimum of 1000 HITs completed.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford CoreNLP (for constituency parses, POS tags, NER tags, dependency parse trees)
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Only 77.3% of correct answers in the development set are constituents in the constituency parse, placing an effective ceiling on accuracy of constituent-based methods. Questions with span-based answers are more constrained than interpretative questions in advanced standardized tests.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development, and testing of machine reading comprehension models. The dataset is partitioned into training (80%), development (10%), and test (10%) sets.

name.evidence: We present the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD), a new reading comprehension dataset consisting of 100,000+ questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles

description.evidence: SQuAD contains 107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 articles, and is almost two orders of magnitude larger than previous manually labeled RC datasets such as MCTest

url.evidence: The dataset is freely available at https://stanford-qa.com

creator.evidence: Pranav Rajpurkar and Jian Zhang and Konstantin Lopyrev and Percy Liang ... Computer Science Department, Stanford University

inLanguage.evidence: we used Project Nayuki's Wikipedia's internal PageRanks to obtain the top 10000 articles of English Wikipedia

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We collect our dataset in three stages: curating passages, crowdsourcing question-answers on those passages, and obtaining additional answers.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: we used Project Nayuki's Wikipedia's internal PageRanks to obtain the top 10000 articles of English Wikipedia... We used the Daemo platform (Gaikwad et al., 2015), with Amazon Mechanical Turk as its backend.

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: Over the development and test sets, 2.6% of questions were marked unanswerable by at least one of the additional crowdworkers.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: we used Project Nayuki's Wikipedia's internal PageRanks to obtain the top 10000 articles of English Wikipedia, from which we sampled 536 articles uniformly at random. From each of these articles, we extracted individual paragraphs, stripping away images, figures, tables, and discarding paragraphs shorter than 500 characters. The result was 23,215 paragraphs for the 536 articles

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: From each of these articles, we extracted individual paragraphs, stripping away images, figures, tables, and discarding paragraphs shorter than 500 characters... We partitioned the articles randomly into a training set (80%), a development set (10%), and a test set (10%).

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: On each paragraph, crowdworkers were tasked with asking and answering up to 5 questions on the content of that paragraph. The questions had to be entered in a text field, and the answers had to be highlighted in the paragraph... crowdworkers were encouraged to ask questions in their own words, without copying word phrases from the paragraph.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: We used the Daemo platform (Gaikwad et al., 2015), with Amazon Mechanical Turk as its backend.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: To evaluate human performance, we treat the second answer to each question as the human prediction, and keep the other answers as ground truth answers. The resulting human performance score on the test set is 77.0% for the exact match metric, and 86.8% for F1. Mismatch occurs mostly due to inclusion/exclusion of non-essential phrases

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: we obtained at least 2 additional answers for each question in the development and test sets... each of the questions in these sets has at least three answers

rai:annotatorDemographics.evidence: Crowdworkers were required to have a 97% HIT acceptance rate, a minimum of 1000 HITs, and be located in the United States or Canada.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: The non-numerical answers are categorized using constituency parses and POS tags generated by Stanford CoreNLP. The proper noun phrases are further split into person, location and other entities using NER tags.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: Ignoring punctuation and articles, we find that 77.3% of the correct answers in the development set are constituents. This places an effective ceiling on the accuracy of our methods... questions with span-based answers are more constrained than the more interpretative questions found in more advanced standardized tests

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We have made our dataset freely available to encourage exploration of more expressive models... We partitioned the articles randomly into a training set (80%), a development set (10%), and a test set (10%).
